# Memories and Caches

## Concepts

A memory contract includes width, depth, port count, read latency, write masks, initialization, and read-during-write behavior. These choices are visible to clients even when the implementation changes.

An RTL array can become registers, FPGA block RAM, or an ASIC memory macro. Simulation of an array does not demonstrate that synthesis will select an efficient memory. A cache additionally needs tag storage, valid state, replacement policy, and behavior for misses; the storage implementation must support those operations.

## Implementation

Keep storage behind an explicit wrapper with address, enables, data, masks, and a defined response timing. An FPGA backend may infer RAM; an ASIC backend may instantiate an SRAM macro. Both should satisfy the same externally documented contract.

For a macro, collect its simulation model, Liberty timing model, LEF abstraction, and layout view. Fixed dimensions and pin locations affect floorplanning. Do not reset every array element merely to obtain convenient simulation behavior: determine what reset or initialization the intended memory technology supports.

When studying a processor cache, inventory data arrays and tag arrays separately. Identify how their latency interacts with the pipeline and how invalidation differs from clearing stored data.

## Hands-on Experiments

Specify a small synchronous memory and test read latency, masked writes, same-address read/write, boundary addresses, and initialization assumptions. Synthesize it for a selected FPGA target and a generic logic target; inspect whether the reports show RAM resources or registers.

Create a second wrapper for a chosen macro model and rerun the interface tests. Compare implementation reports only after confirming that both wrappers implement the same semantics. Record macro provenance and all required integration views.
